      Family: Ostreidae

nodes.title: Value
nodes.body:
Commercial: In 1987, 39.8 million pounds of oyster meat valued at $92.4 million were landed in the United States. The Gulf of Mexico region, lead principally by Louisiana with 65% of the region, produced 18.4 million pounds (512). In Texas, oyster season is generally open from November 1 to April 30, except in portions of Laguna Madre. Licenses are necessary for oyster dredges. Oysters need t o be 3 inches or larger, with commercial vessels limited to not more than 50 barrels. Oysters may be taken only from water approved by the Texas State Commissioner of Health (721). The Texas Parks and Wildlife Department has recently developed a fishery management plan to limit the catch and time of catch for oysters (578).

Recreational: In Texas, oysters can be collected for personal use with hand, tongs, or sport dredges (smaller than 14 inches in width); larger dredges require licenses. Only oysters greater than 3 inches can be taken from waters approved by the Texas State Commissioner of Health from November 1 to April 30. There is no closed season south of Port Mansfield channel in the Laguna Madre (722).

Ecological Role: Oysters are important in providing reef habitats that serve as areas of concentration for many other organisms (761 25). They compete for space with other bivalves, namely Crepidula, Anomia, Ischadium (630 428). Troublesome boring organisms reduce the market value, as well as consume energy in shell growth and repair; the most common of which are Cliona, the boring sponge and Diplothyra smithii the boring crab.

Indicator: Broutman and Leonard (61) review the methodology and problems of water classification, predominantly based on fecal coliform bacteria, for shellfish throughout the Gulf of Mexico. Oysters are often used for pesticide and petroleum byproduct LD-50 analyses.

nodes.title: Range
nodes.body:
Overall: Crassostrea virginica occurs from the Gulf of St. Lawrence to the Yucatan peninsula of Mexico and t o Venezuela. It is abundant in the estuaries along the Gulf of Mexico; in addition it has concentration centers in Chesapeake Bay and Long Island Sound.

Within Study Area: The American oyster is predominant in the estuaries from Texas t o Florida along the Gulf coast; Louisiana and Texas, east of Corpus Christi, have the highest concentrations.

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body:
Eggs/Larva: Eggs and early larval stages are planktonic.
Larva: Larvae settle out as veligers, crawling along the sediment surface until they find a suitable substrate to attach. Larvae are gregarious enabling oysters to form extensive reefs over long periods of time.
Adults: Adults are sedentary, cemented to the original spot the spat settled on.

nodes.title: Habitat
nodes.body:
Type: Eggs are planktonic. Larvae are meroplanktonic to benthic. Juveniles (spat) and adults are sessile, benthic. All stages are estuarine.

Substrate: The preferred habitats are shallow bays, other oyster shell and hard surfaces, mud flats and offshore sand bars (86 137 459). Oyster reefs are typically on hard bottoms, oysters are also abundant on surrounding mud bottoms. Maximum setting occurs on horizontal surfaces (125). Harry (284) demonstrated that oysters thrive on bottoms consisting of 17-100 % sand.

nodes.title: Physical/chemical
nodes.body:
Temperature: There may be as many as three races of American oyster based on temperature regimes (7). {Buroker, et al. (84) found all oysters to be genetically equivalent; and Groue and Lester (245) found the Laguna Madre oysters to be genetically distinct from four other Gulf populations.} This feature may be reflected in spawning temperatures determined by
Stauber (673).  Gulf of Mexico oysters spawn around 25 C (water temperatures must be consistently over 20 C and above 25 C for mass spawnings); there are two races on the East Coast that spawn at 16 and 20 C. Adults exist within the range of -2 C in New England to 36 C in the Gulf of Mexico . During low tide oysters can withstand temperatures below freezing and above 49 C (227). Cake (90) reports that Gulf oysters are not as tolerant of freezing as the East Coast race.

Salinity: Adults in the Gulf of Mexico normally occur at salinities from 10-30 ppt, tolerating a range from 2-40 ppt (266). Eleutrius (199) found salinities from 2-22 ppt from areas of productive reefs. Gunter (259) reported high mortalities during spring floods in Mississippi Sound and Louisiana {see also Burrell (85) for Mobile Bay (May 1972) and Santee
River, South Carolina}. Oysters from the Laguna Madre of Texas tolerate higher salinities, growing and spawning in salinities greater than 40 ppt (71). Spat setting is usually less at low salinities (459 108), while Chanley reports that optimum growth for spat is 15-22 ppt.

Oxygen: Oysters are facultative anaerobes, enabling them to withstand periods of low or no oxygen. Consumption of oxygen is a function of the salinity and temperature of the water.

Movements and Migrations
Since the adults are sessile their distribution is determined by larval stages and subsequent survival of the spat. Spat and adult oysters in restricted waters are often moved to leased lots in approved waters for depuration and or to increase the abundance in that area space for future harvests.

nodes.title: Reproduction
nodes.body:
Repro Mode: Adults are protandrous hermaphrodites, but dioecious. The male releases sperm and a pheromone into the water column that can be detected by the females at the inhalent siphon, triggering the release of eggs for external fertilization (15).

Season: In the northern Gulf of Mexico, spawning occurs from March to November (86). Peaks occur in Louisiana in late May to early June and September (562). In Mississippi, spawning occurs from May to October with a peak in June (428). In south Texas, Copeland and Hoese (137) report spawning occurs in all months except July and August, because of temperature.

Reproductive Capacity: Each female produces 23-86 million eggs proportional to the size of the female. Females may spawn several times within a season (168).

Growth and Development
Egg: The eggs hatch 6 hours after fertilization at a temperature of 24 c (416).

Larvae: Larvae remain in the water column 2-3 weeks after hatching, passing through several developmental stages {trochophore, prodissoconchI, II (pediveliger)}.

Juvenile: Juveniles, called spat, develop when larvae cement themselves to the substrate. Fastest growth occurs during the first 3 months (24).

Adult: In the Gulf of Mexico, sexual maturity may be reached as soon as 4 weeks after attachment (458), but generally 18-24 months is normal (578). Butler (86) reports growth for the Gulf oysters to be approximately 50 mm/y. Gunter (258) gives growth rates of -26-.30 mm/day in the first 3 months, 60 mm in the first year, 90 mm in the second year and 115 mm in the three years. Growth coefficients in the Louisiana are highly variable fluctuating from .42 to .86 mm/day (234). Growth is greatest in August and September, after spawning when glycogen reserves are restored (417 572).

Food and Feeding
Larva: Larvae feed on plankton (247).
Juvenile/Adult: Juvenile sand adults are filter feeders particularly effective around the 3-4 range (287). Naked flagellates are preferred. Bacteria are taken as a minor component of the diet. Oysters have variable uptake of carbon from spartina alterniflora crude fiber ranging from less than 1% in Chesapeake area to over 20% in the southeast region - primarily due to differences in crude fiber concentrations in the seston (155).

Ecological Interactions and Notes
Oyster Larvae are susceptible to a large variety of filter feeders. The predatory snail, Thais haemastoma, is responsible for the majority of oyster mortalities in Louisiana, Mississippi and Alabama (106). Other predators include the lightning whelk, Busycon contrarium; blue crab, Callinectes sapidus; stone crab, Menippe adina; and the black drum, Pogonias cromis (102 90).

Oysters infested with burrowing clams and sponges have been indicated t o be much more susceptible to predation by black drum and possibly other predators because of weakened shells (102) - Intertidal oysters because of their slower growth, thicker shells, and relative time under water seem to be less susceptible to this predation than their deeper water counterparts.  Price (573) discussed the various development, shapes and location of oyster reefs with respect to shoreline, channels and distance from the Gulf. Reefs grow from the shoreline out; as a current is encountered the reef turns to a right angle and parallels the current, eventually turning back on itself. Other reefs grow parallel to channels.

Repro Mode: Adults are protandrous hermaphrodites, but dioecious. The male releases sperm and a pheromone into the water column that can be detected by the females at the inhalent siphon, triggering the release of eggs for external fertilization (15).

Season: In the northern Gulf of Mexico, spawning occurs from March to November (86). Peaks occur in Louisiana in late May to early June and September (562). In Mississippi, spawning occurs from May to October with a peak in June (428). In south Texas, Copeland and Hoese (137) report spawning occurs in all months except July and August, because of temperature.

Reproductive Capacity: Each female produces 23-86 million eggs proportional to the size of the female. Females may spawn several times within a season (168).

Growth and Development
Egg: The eggs hatch 6 hours after fertilization at a temperature of 24 c (416).

Larvae: Larvae remain in the water column 2-3 weeks after hatching, passing through several developmental stages {trochophore, prodissoconchI, II (pediveliger)}.

Juvenile: Juveniles, called spat, develop when larvae cement themselves to the substrate. Fastest growth occurs during the first 3 months (24).

Adult: In the Gulf of Mexico, sexual maturity may be reached as soon as 4 weeks after attachment (458), but generally 18-24 months is normal (578). Butler (86) reports growth for the Gulf oysters to be approximately 50 mm/y. Gunter (258) gives growth rates of -26-.30 mm/day in the first 3 months, 60 mm in the first year, 90 mm in the second year and 115 mm in the three years. Growth coefficients in the Louisiana are highly variable fluctuating from .42 to .86 mm/day (234). Growth is greatest in August and September, after spawning when glycogen reserves are restored (417 572).

Food and Feeding
Larva: Larvae feed on plankton (247).
Juvenile/Adult: Juvenile sand adults are filter feeders particularly effective around the 3-4 range (287). Naked flagellates are preferred. Bacteria are taken as a minor component of the diet. Oysters have variable uptake of carbon from spartina alterniflora crude fiber ranging from less than 1% in Chesapeake area to over 20% in the southeast region - primarily due to differences in crude fiber concentrations in the seston (155).

Ecological Interactions and Notes
Oyster Larvae are susceptible to a large variety of filter feeders. The predatory snail, Thais haemastoma, is responsible for the majority of oyster mortalities in Louisiana, Mississippi and Alabama (106). Other predators include the lightning whelk, Busycon contrarium; blue crab, Callinectes sapidus; stone crab, Menippe adina; and the black drum, Pogonias cromis (102 90).

Oysters infested with burrowing clams and sponges have been indicated t o be much more susceptible to predation by black drum and possibly other predators because of weakened shells (102) - Intertidal oysters because of their slower growth, thicker shells, and relative time under water seem to be less susceptible to this predation than their deeper water counterparts.  Price (573) discussed the various development, shapes and location of oyster reefs with respect to shoreline, channels and distance from the Gulf. Reefs grow from the shoreline out; as a current is encountered the reef turns to a right angle and parallels the current, eventually turning back on itself. Other reefs grow parallel to channels.
